projectTasks.title: Library catalogue system — Part A: the catalogue
projectTasks.brief:
A library is building a catalogue system, split into three parts — each part builds directly on the code you write for the one before it, so keep what you've written rather than starting over.

**Part A.** Write a function `catalogue_line(title, author)` that returns the formatted string `<title> by <author>`. Input a whole number N, then N books, each as a title then an author, storing them in two parallel lists. Print every book's catalogue line, one per line, using your function.
hints: Build both lists together in one loop, then loop again afterwards to print each line using your function.
def catalogue_line(title, author): return f"{title} by {author}" — then for i in range(n): print(catalogue_line(titles[i], authors[i])).

projectTasks.title: Library catalogue system — Part B: searching
projectTasks.brief: **Part B.** Your code carries on from Part A — keep everything you already wrote and add to it. No new setup input needed — reuse the lists you already built. Write a function `find_book(title)` that returns the matching author if `title` is in your titles list, otherwise `None`. Input a title to search for. If found, print `Found: <title> by <author>`; otherwise print `Not found`.
hints: Don't delete your Part A code — reuse the titles and authors lists you already have.
def find_book(title): if title in titles: return authors[titles.index(title)]; return None — then check the result with if/else.

tests.expect:
Dune by Herbert
1984 by Orwell
Found: Dune by Herbert

Dune by Herbert
1984 by Orwell
Not found

projectTasks.title: Library catalogue system — Part C: copies available
projectTasks.brief: **Part C.** Keep everything from Parts A and B. Input a whole number for how many copies are available. If the search in Part B found a book, print an extra line, `Copies: <n>`. If it didn't, print nothing more.
hints: Always read the copies number, but only print the extra line inside the same if-branch where Part B found a match.
copies = int(input()); if author: print(f"Copies: {copies}") — added after your existing Part B lines.

tests.expect:
Dune by Herbert
1984 by Orwell
Found: Dune by Herbert
Copies: 3

Dune by Herbert
1984 by Orwell
Not found

projectTasks.title: Password manager — Part A: strength check
projectTasks.brief:
A website is building a simple password manager, split into three parts — each part builds directly on the code you write for the one before it.

**Part A.** Write a function `is_strong(pw)` that returns True if `pw` is at least 8 characters long **and** contains at least one digit, otherwise False. Input a whole number N, then N sites, each as a site name then a password, storing them in two parallel lists. Print each site's status, one per line, in the format `<site>: Strong` or `<site>: Weak`.
hints: any(ch.isdigit() for ch in pw) is True if at least one character is a digit.
def is_strong(pw): return len(pw) >= 8 and any(ch.isdigit() for ch in pw) — then loop over both lists together printing each status.

projectTasks.title: Password manager — Part B: a summary count
projectTasks.brief: **Part B.** Your code carries on from Part A — keep everything you already wrote and add to it. No new input needed. After your Part A lines, print how many passwords are strong, then how many are weak, in the format `Strong: <n>` then `Weak: <n>`.
hints: Don't delete your Part A code — reuse is_strong() and the passwords list you already have.
strong_count = sum(1 for pw in passwords if is_strong(pw)); weak_count = n - strong_count.

tests.expect:
Email: Strong
Bank: Weak
Strong: 1
Weak: 1

projectTasks.title: Password manager — Part C: look up a site
projectTasks.brief: **Part C.** Keep everything from Parts A and B. Write a function `lookup(site)` that returns the matching password if `site` is in your sites list, otherwise `None`. Input a site to search for. If found, print `<site> password is Strong` or `<site> password is Weak` using is_strong(); otherwise print `Site not found`.
hints: lookup() mirrors find_book() from the library project — same pattern, different data.
def lookup(site): if site in sites: return passwords[sites.index(site)]; return None — then use is_strong() on the result if it isn't None.

tests.expect:
Email: Strong
Bank: Weak
Strong: 1
Weak: 1
Email password is Strong

Shop: Strong
Strong: 1
Weak: 0
Site not found

projectTasks.title: Quiz score tracker — Part A: the average
projectTasks.brief:
A teacher is building a quiz score tracker, split into three parts — each part builds directly on the code you write for the one before it.

**Part A.** Write a function `average(scores)` that returns the mean of a list, rounded to 1 decimal place. Input a whole number N, then N whole-number scores, storing them in a list. Print the average using your function, in the format `Average: <n>`.
hints: Build the list with a loop or a list comprehension, then pass the whole list into your function.
def average(scores): return round(sum(scores) / len(scores), 1).

projectTasks.title: Quiz score tracker — Part B: saving to a file
projectTasks.brief: **Part B.** Your code carries on from Part A — keep everything you already wrote and add to it. No new input needed. Write every score to `quiz_log.txt`, one per line. Print `Saved to quiz_log.txt` as a new line.
hints: Don't delete your Part A code — reuse the scores list you already built.
with open("quiz_log.txt", "w") as f: for s in scores: f.write(str(s) + "\n") — then print the confirmation line.

projectTasks.title: Quiz score tracker — Part C: pass or fail
projectTasks.brief: **Part C.** Keep everything from Parts A and B. No new input needed. Write a function `pass_count(vals)` that returns how many values in a list are 50 or more. Reopen `quiz_log.txt`, reading the scores back as numbers. Print how many passed, then how many failed, in the format `Passed: <n>` then `Failed: <n>`.
hints: Reopen the file and cast each line back to a whole number before counting.
with open("quiz_log.txt", "r") as f: reloaded = [int(line.strip()) for line in f] — then def pass_count(vals): return sum(1 for v in vals if v >= 50).

tests.expect:
Average: 70.0
Saved to quiz_log.txt
Passed: 3
Failed: 0

Average: 55.0
Saved to quiz_log.txt
Passed: 2
Failed: 1

projectTasks.title: Adventure inventory — Part A: starting items
projectTasks.brief:
A text adventure game needs an inventory system, split into three parts — each part builds directly on the code you write for the one before it.

**Part A.** Write a function `add_item(inv, item)` that appends `item` to the list `inv`. Input a whole number N, then N item names, adding each to an inventory list using your function. Print the inventory as one line, in the format `Inventory: <item>, <item>, ...`.
hints: Your function changes the list in place with .append() — it doesn't need to return anything.
def add_item(inv, item): inv.append(item) — then print("Inventory: " + ", ".join(inventory)).

projectTasks.title: Adventure inventory — Part B: using an item
projectTasks.brief: **Part B.** Your code carries on from Part A — keep everything you already wrote and add to it. Write a function `remove_item(inv, item)` that removes the first entry matching `item` (ignoring upper/lower case) and returns True, or returns False if nothing matched. Input an item name to use. Print `Used <item>` if it was removed, otherwise `You don't have that`.
hints: Compare .lower() on both sides so "Potion" matches "potion" in the inventory.
def remove_item(inv, item): for entry in inv: if entry.lower() == item.lower(): inv.remove(entry); return True; return False.

tests.expect:
Inventory: sword, shield, potion
Used Potion

Inventory: key, map
You don't have that

projectTasks.title: Adventure inventory — Part C: carry weight
projectTasks.brief: **Part C.** Keep everything from Parts A and B. Write a function `total_weight(weights)` that returns the sum of a list. Input one whole-number weight for each item currently left in the inventory (after Part B's use), then a whole-number weight limit. Print the total weight and whether it's within the limit, in the format `Total weight: <n> (OK)` or `Total weight: <n> (Over limit!)`.
hints: Read one weight per item still in the inventory, in the same order the inventory list is in now.
weights = [int(input()) for _ in inventory]; limit = int(input()); total = total_weight(weights); "OK" if total <= limit else "Over limit!".

tests.expect:
Inventory: sword, shield, potion
Used Potion
Total weight: 8 (OK)

Inventory: key, map
You don't have that
Total weight: 10 (Over limit!)

projectTasks.title: Class seating planner — Part A: an empty grid
projectTasks.brief:
A teacher is building a seating planner, split into three parts — each part builds directly on the code you write for the one before it.

**Part A.** Write a function `display(grid)` that prints each row of a 2D list as space-separated values. Input a number of rows R, then a number of columns C. Build a grid of R rows by C columns, every seat starting as `-`, and display it with your function.
hints: A list of lists, built with a nested list comprehension, all starting as "-".
grid = [["-" for _ in range(c)] for _ in range(r)] — then def display(grid): for row in grid: print(" ".join(row)).

projectTasks.title: Class seating planner — Part B: assigning a seat
projectTasks.brief: **Part B.** Your code carries on from Part A — keep everything you already wrote and add to it. Write a function `assign_seat(grid, row, col, name)` that places the first letter of `name` into that seat and returns True if the seat was empty, otherwise returns False and changes nothing. Input a student's name, then a row and a column (both starting from 0). Print `Seated` or `Seat taken`, then redisplay the grid using your Part A function.
hints: Only change the grid if the seat is currently "-" — check before you assign.
def assign_seat(grid, row, col, name): if grid[row][col] == "-": grid[row][col] = name[0]; return True; return False — then call display(grid) again afterwards.

projectTasks.title: Class seating planner — Part C: checking a seat
projectTasks.brief: **Part C.** Keep everything from Parts A and B. Write a function `is_empty(grid, row, col)` that returns True if that seat is `-`, otherwise False. Input a row and a column to check. Print `Empty` or `Taken`.
hints: A one-line function comparing the grid cell to "-".
def is_empty(grid, row, col): return grid[row][col] == "-" — then print based on the result.

projectTasks.title: Budget tracker — Part A: total by category
projectTasks.brief:
Someone is tracking their spending by category, split into three parts — each part builds directly on the code you write for the one before it.

**Part A.** Write a function `total_for(cats, amts, target)` that adds up every amount whose matching category equals `target`. Input a whole number N, then N transactions, each as a category then an amount (which may include pence), storing them in two parallel lists. Input a category to total up. Print the result in the format `<category>: £<amount>`.
hints: Loop through both lists together by index, adding an amount whenever its category matches.
def total_for(cats, amts, target): total = 0; for i in range(len(cats)): if cats[i] == target: total += amts[i]; return total.

projectTasks.title: Budget tracker — Part B: a summary file
projectTasks.brief: **Part B.** Your code carries on from Part A — keep everything you already wrote and add to it. No new input needed. Work out every category that appears (each one once), then write a line for each to `budget.txt`, in the format `<category>: £<total>`, using your total_for() function. Print `Saved summary to budget.txt` as a new line.
hints: Build a list of the categories that appear, each only once, before writing anything to the file.
unique_cats = []; for c in cats: if c not in unique_cats: unique_cats.append(c) — then write one line per unique category using total_for().

projectTasks.title: Budget tracker — Part C: biggest spend
projectTasks.brief: **Part C.** Keep everything from Parts A and B. No new input needed. Write a function `highest_category(lines)` that takes the lines read back from a file (each in the format `<category>: £<amount>`), and returns the name of the category with the highest amount. Reopen `budget.txt` and print the result in the format `Highest: <category>`.
hints: Split each line on ": £" to separate the category name from the amount, casting the amount to a float before comparing.
name, amount = line.strip().split(": £") — keep track of the best name and amount seen so far as you loop through the reopened file's lines.

tests.expect:
Food: £30.0
Saved summary to budget.txt
Highest: Food

Fun: £20.0
Saved summary to budget.txt
Highest: Fun
